questions.q: What is the basic recipe for writing a custom nn.Module layer with its own learnable parameters?
options: Define parameters globally outside any class, then reference them in a standalone function
Create nn.Parameter instances in __init__ (assigned as attributes) and implement the computation in forward()
Subclass torch.Tensor directly and override its arithmetic operators
Use nn.Sequential exclusively; custom logic is not supported
questions.explain: This is the same core pattern from Lesson 8: assign nn.Parameter instances as attributes inside __init__ (so nn.Module's auto-discovery picks them up), then use them in forward() to define the layer's computation.

questions.q: What does register_buffer do, and how does it differ from nn.Parameter?
options: It is identical to nn.Parameter in every respect
It registers a tensor that moves with the model via .to(device) and is saved in state_dict(), but is never included in .parameters() and never updated by the optimizer
It permanently deletes a tensor from memory
It only works for tensors already on the GPU
questions.explain: register_buffer tracks a tensor for device-moving and serialization purposes, like a parameter, but explicitly excludes it from .parameters() and gradient-based updates -- appropriate for non-learnable state like a running average.

questions.q: What goes wrong if you store a list of submodules as a plain Python list attribute (self.blocks = [Block(), Block()]) instead of nn.ModuleList?
options: Nothing; plain lists and nn.ModuleList behave identically

nn.Module's attribute-scanning never discovers those submodules, so their parameters are silently excluded from .parameters(), they don't move with .to(device), and they're missing from state_dict() -- with no error raised
The code immediately raises a TypeError at model construction
The submodules train twice as fast
questions.explain: A plain Python list is invisible to nn.Module's parameter/submodule discovery mechanism. This is a dangerous silent bug: the model runs without error, but those layers never receive gradient updates, never move devices, and are absent from checkpoints.

questions.q: Why would you build a small reusable 'block' module (e.g. MLPBlock combining Linear + ReLU) rather than always using nn.Sequential directly?
options: nn.Sequential cannot contain more than two layers

A custom block lets you package and reuse a multi-layer pattern as one named unit, and compose more complex logic (branching, loops, variable depth) that a straight-line nn.Sequential stack can't express
Blocks run faster than nn.Sequential on every hardware configuration
nn.Sequential does not support activation functions
questions.explain: nn.Sequential is limited to a straight-line chain of layers. A custom nn.Module block can be reused across a model (e.g. inside a loop building variable depth) and can express logic nn.Sequential alone cannot, such as branching or custom forward control flow.

questions.q: What three things does assigning an nn.Parameter as a module attribute get you automatically, 'for free'?
options: Faster CPU execution, smaller file size, and automatic batch size tuning
Discovery by .parameters()/.named_parameters(), gradient tracking through autograd, and inclusion in state_dict() for saving/loading
Automatic conversion to float16, automatic GPU placement, and automatic normalization
A guaranteed reduction in loss during training
questions.explain: Because nn.Module scans its attributes for nn.Parameter instances, assigning one gets it automatically included in .parameters() (and therefore optimizers), tracked by autograd via requires_grad=True, and saved/restored through state_dict().
